content: In early life, stunting affects up to half of all adolescents in some countries. Micronutrient malnutrition, particularly deficiencies in iron, iodine, and vitamin A, is highly prevalent among adolescents and significantly impacts their overall health. Approximately two-thirds of premature deaths and one-third of the total disease burden in adulthood are linked to environmental factors, conditions, or behaviors established during adolescence. Globally, there are 2 million largely preventable adolescent deaths annually, with malnutrition playing a role as either a direct cause or an exacerbating factor. Most adolescent deaths occur in lowand middle-income countries, particularly in Africa (45%) and Southeast Asia (26%), despite these regions hosting only 19% and 30% of the global adolescent population, respectively. Overweight and obesity in adolescents, often resulting from unhealthy diets and insufficient physical activity, increase the risk of future non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as diabetes, hypertension, coronary heart disease, stroke, certain cancers, and obstructive sleep apnea. Globally, the leading contributors to disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) in adolescents include iron deficiency anemia, particularly in the 10–14 age group, with the highest prevalence in South East Asia, Europe, the Western Pacific, and high-income countries. Iron deficiency anemia is also widespread in Africa, the Eastern Mediterranean, and the Americas. Inadequate nutrition, combined with rapid physical growth during early adolescence, menstruation, and infections causing blood loss (e.g., hookworm, malaria, and urinary schistosomiasis), contributes to iron depletion and deficiency in adolescents. Other major contributors to DALYs in younger adolescents (10–14 years) include lower respiratory infections (e.g., influenza, pneumococcal pneumonia, Haemophilus influenzae type B), diarrheal diseases, anxiety disorders, and meningitis. Among older adolescents (15–19 years), leading contributors include depressive disorders, maternal conditions (e.g., hemorrhage, sepsis, hypertensive disorders, obstructed labor, complications of abortion, and maternal deaths aggravated by AIDS or tuberculosis), self-harm, and anxiety disorders. Evidence-based interventions and policies for improving adolescent nutrition require government leadership, adolescent participation, adequate financing, and national accountability. Effective adolescent health programming involves assessing needs, analyzing the landscape, and setting priorities to implement tailored policies and interventions. Well-nourished adolescents protected from disease, infection, and early pregnancy are less likely to experience malnutrition in all its forms during adolescence and adulthood. They are also more likely to avoid NCDs, achieve optimal maternal and birth outcomes, and enjoy increased productivity. The conceptual framework of malnutrition identifies underlying causes such as household food insecurity, inadequate feeding and care practices, and environmental and health service factors. To achieve health and well-being, adolescents must have access to nutritious diets, engage in positive health behaviors, and access essential health services. Eight evidence-based nutrition interventions and policies have been identified to improve adolescent nutrition, including promoting healthy diets, physical activity, disease prevention, and managing acute malnutrition. Healthy diets play a critical role in preventing all forms of malnutrition and reducing the risk of cardiovascular diseases, type 2 diabetes, and certain cancers. A healthy diet includes adequate energy, protein, vitamins, and minerals from foods such as fruits, vegetables, legumes, nuts, and whole grains, while limiting free sugars, unhealthy fats, and sodium. However, many adolescents consume insufficient fruits, vegetables, and whole grains while consuming excessive fats, sodium, cholesterol, and added sugars. Barriers to healthy diets include physical, economic, and socio-cultural factors, as well as a lack of knowledge and self-efficacy. Eating disorders, such as anorexia nervosa and bulimia, often begin in adolescence, particularly among girls, and are associated with serious physical and mental health outcomes, including depression, anxiety, and substance abuse. Adolescents are increasingly exposed to unhealthy food environments and aggressive marketing of nutrient-poor, energy-dense foods high in sugar, sodium, and fat. They often lack access to affordable fresh fruits and vegetables and may not have the knowledge or resources to prepare healthy meals. Micronutrient deficiencies, particularly in iron, folic acid, vitamin A, and vitamin B12, are common among adolescents. Iron deficiency anemia is the leading cause of DALYs for adolescents globally, reducing physical capacity and work performance. Entering pregnancy with suboptimal iron reserves increases the risk of adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. Iodine deficiency disorders are the second-largest micronutrient burden among adolescents, particularly in South Asia, sub-Saharan Africa, and the Middle East. Vitamin A deficiency is also a significant global health concern. Fortification of staple foods and targeted supplementation can help address these deficiencies, especially in settings where access to diverse, nutrient-rich diets is limited. WHO recommendations emphasize the importance of fortifying staple foods such as maize flour, cornmeal, and salt with essential micronutrients like iron, folic acid, and iodine. Daily or intermittent iron and folic acid supplementation is recommended for menstruating adolescent girls and women in areas with high anemia prevalence. These interventions should complement efforts to promote healthy diets and address the specific nutritional needs of adolescents.
